In the farming tradition, every farm generally has a private threshing floor on which to carry out these activities, but in some villages there are public ones that the whole community may use. fold, pleat. Also called pleche. Besides the general meaning (la chieche di la onne o di lu calzone: the pleat of the skirt or of the trousers), the word chieche (or pleche) is also used to refer to a generous portion of sausage (na chieche di salcicce). Sausages, in order to dry, were hung on wooden sticks placed high up, in rooms with little humidity (usually the kitchen). As they dried, the part resting on the stick and the opposite part shrank, thus forming a fold

butcher's shop. An archaic term almost out of use, imported from Naples. The origin of the word is to be sought in Low Latin, and in particular in the term "planca" (plank, wooden board), which in Neapolitan became "chianca". Since butchered meat was originally displayed and sold at retail resting on a wooden table (a plank, precisely), the etymology of the word is easy to trace: the butcher's shop is a place where one or more wooden boards are found

slippers, house shoes. This is perhaps the most fitting occasion to restore to the Abruzzese dialect the "paternity" of this word, which has always, quite wrongly, been attributed to the dialect of Ciociaria (Lazio-Frosinone). On the basis of this unfounded assumption, the term is then ascribed to the Abruzzese dialect as a borrowing from the Ciociaro one. In fact, the aforementioned area of the Frosinone district owes its name to the dialect word "ciocia", which denotes precisely a kind of rustic footwear made of a single piece fastened to the foot by means of leather or cloth straps. But the term "ciocia" derives from the Abruzzese "chiochie", inherited directly from Latin

conjugated only in the third person singular of some tenses of the indicative and, much more rarely, in the past participle, present participle and gerund. This particular verb has no infinitive form. It is surprising that through the passing of the centuries the verb in question has kept its Latin root ferre absolutely unchanged (paradigm: fero-fers-tuli-latum-ferre). And not only that: of the Latin verb cited, the irregular form has also remained intact (from which derives, in the dialect term, the abolition of the infinitive mood). Anyone who in their school years grappled with translations from Latin will remember with particular impatience this difficult verb which, among the thousand exceptions concerning it, also counts the "misfortune" of having an almost unlimited number of meanings (certainly not helpful when translating during a class test…). Among those meanings there are some that well justify the current one in our dialect: to spread, to scatter, to drag along, to divulge, to burst in, to carry away. All senses that suit the action of the wind perfectly

trap for catching or killing edible or fur-bearing wild animals. Usually it consisted of a rather heavy stone that fell on the prey. In Fallo, in the locality "Lu Cucù", there is one for catching foxes. It consists of two large flat stones laid one on top of the other, one of which was raised on one side and held up by a wooden stick. The bait (usually meat) was placed under the stick. When the fox tried to pull the meat away, it knocked down the stick and the stone fell on it, crushing it

it is difficult to find an exact equivalent in Italian. The term denotes a medium-sized cloth, often square, used mostly as a "container" for small-scale gathering of farm produce: once the cloth is filled, the four corners are brought together at the top and knotted to keep the contents from spilling out. But the term also denotes many other similar "cloths": an improvised kitchen apron, a coarse napkin, a large handkerchief used to make a bundle, etc. Figuratively, the "mandricchie" is "the initial form" of what will become a bundle (the "multine") or a wrapping (the "mappatelle"). While finding the exact Italian equivalent is a hard task, the etymology of the word is easily traced to the Latin feminine noun "mantica": in ancient Rome it denoted the bag meant to hold provisions for a journey

Derived from the other, very similar dialect term attintà (to feel, to handle), which in turn comes from the Italian attentato (past participle of attentare), to try, to lay hands on. In legal language it is also used in place of assault, aggression. When fruit-tree growing was still very active, when children were taken to the fields it was customary to show them the fruit as it ripened. The children's curiosity led them to touch the fruit, but they were promptly admonished with the phrase: "Nin li tuccuà ca sinnò zi matente!" (do not touch them, otherwise they get spoiled)

shapeless, ungainly thing. At first glance the term would seem to derive from the Italian phrase "mazzo di affari" (that is, a jumble of things thrown together), of which it might be a contraction. Another, far more credible hypothesis is that the term is the union of two Latin words: massa and fere. The first, similar to the Italian, corresponds to a mass, a heap, while the second (fere) means roughly, almost, generally. Obviously, as always happens in these cases, through the various passages (from Latin to Italian and from Italian to dialect) the terms underwent a series of transformations, becoming precisely "mazzuàffere" while leaving the concept unchanged: an ugly, ungainly thing

uncultivated field, in a state of abandonment. The etymology of this word is astonishing: it derives from the Italian term "nicchia" not in its most common sense (recess), but in the very learned one which, in ecology, specifically indicates the place where the environmental factors suited to the growth of a species occur. The "nnicchiere" is therefore a kind of ecological microcosm in which all the vital conditions allowing the spontaneous (wild) growth of plants have come about naturally. The Italian term in question derives from the verb "nicchiare" (again in the field of ecological science), which in turn derives from the Vulgar Latin "nidiculare", that is, to show hostility (a wild appearance): the same shown by a "nnicchiere" covered in brambles

In dialect the term is used in the feminine and, by allegory, refers to the decorative "knot" with which a ribbon is tied to make a finocce: stone, seed of a fruit, olive pomace

little, in a minimal quantity. This term is decidedly bizarre and, especially in its more contracted form, skilfully hides its etymology. The meaning indicated does not refer exclusively to a tangible or physical quantity but, like the corresponding Italian idiomatic forms, also to a figurative, moral, qualitative value. The word derives from the Italian "insegna" (and also keeps its feminine gender) in its most archaic meaning of "…(omissis) a mark serving to provide a quantitative reference within specific conventions". By linguistic abuse, the term then came to indicate the "smallest" portion of the aforementioned quantitative reference. Moreover, already in medieval society the common people used to ironically call a meagre quantity of something an "insegna", with clear reference to the indications shown on certain public "signs" (insegne), ordered by decree of the feudal lords, which bore the cost of certain products referred to the minimum quantities (so as to contain the cost, at least visually…!)

call used to summon goats. Unlike the other calls meant for farm animals, this odd call did not always meet with success. The reason lies in the particularly exuberant and untameable character of goats, which often, in defiance of every heartfelt "zirì-tè" from their master, climbed up the most unreachable and rugged heights. Many goats were a true "curse" for some shepherds of the time, and above all for the younger ones, who added to the animal's untameability a personal tendency to get distracted and to "slacken" their vigilance. Many of them received daily scoldings from their parents because they lost the goat at pasture or because they came home late owing to the long "chases" after particularly rebellious animals that had escaped their control
